title: A Cooling Cup Practice for Noticing Change
markdown:
# A Cooling Cup Practice for Noticing Change

## What This Practice Asks You To Do

This exercise uses a hot drink as a physical reminder that things change while you are watching them. You do not need to clear your mind, feel calmer, or reach any particular state. The only task is to notice what is different between the first sip and the last few minutes. It works with tea, coffee, hot water, or any warm beverage you already prepare.

Most people move through a morning treating their surroundings as fixed. The cup on the desk seems the same from one moment to the next, even though its temperature, smell, and surface are constantly shifting. This practice draws from the theme of impermanence. Instead of thinking about change as an abstract idea, you watch it happen in a cup you can hold. Because the drink is already part of your routine, you do not have to add a new appointment to your day.

## Step-by-Step Instructions

1. Prepare a hot drink as you normally would. Use a cup or mug you can see clearly. Sit down where you can place the cup in front of you without distraction. Take a normal breath and let your shoulders settle.

2. Before you take the first sip, pause for a few breaths. Notice the temperature of the cup against your hands, the steam rising or not rising, the color of the liquid, and any sound it makes. Name one detail silently, such as steam curling to the left or the handle feeling warm. Do not analyze the detail; simply identify it.

3. Take one sip. Notice the temperature in your mouth and the flavor as it first appears. Pay attention to where the liquid touches your tongue and how the taste changes as you swallow.

4. Set a timer for five minutes. Put the cup down and leave it alone. You may sit with it, look out a window, or do a quiet task nearby, but do not drink again until the timer ends. If your mind wanders to your to-do list, notice that it has wandered and bring your attention back to the room or the cup.

5. When the timer rings, pick up the cup again. Notice what has changed: the surface may be stiller, the steam may be gone, the rim may feel cooler, the liquid may taste different. Name one specific difference without judging whether it is better or worse. If you cannot detect a change, that is also information.

6. Take a final sip if you wish. Notice how the flavor or temperature compares to the first sip. Observe whether your attention feels different now than it did at the start.

7. Put the cup down and end the practice. You do not need to record anything, though you may make a brief note if that helps you remember. There is no correct result to chase.

## A Real Example

Maya makes a mug of black tea at 7:15 a.m. She holds the mug with both hands and sees steam rising in a thin column. The rim feels hot against her palms. She takes one sip and notices heat on her tongue and a sharp, bitter taste. She sets the mug on her desk.

She sets a timer for five minutes and opens her email. Her mind drifts to a message she needs to answer, but she notices the drift and returns to the sound of the keyboard. When the timer sounds, she picks up the mug again. The steam is gone. The rim is warm rather than hot. The tea tastes flatter and less bitter than it did at first. She takes another sip and notices the temperature is now comfortable rather than steaming. She names the change aloud: the tea cooled and the flavor softened. She finishes her morning without needing the tea to stay hot, and she carries that observation into the rest of her day as a quiet reminder that nothing stays exactly the same.

## Making It Fit Your Day

You can repeat this once a day or once a week. If you do not drink hot beverages, substitute any object that changes visibly over a few minutes: a bowl of soup, a melting ice cube, or sunlight moving across a floor. Keep the steps the same: notice the first state, wait, notice the new state, and name one difference.

If five minutes feels too long, use two minutes. If you forget to time it, observe the cup when you naturally return to it. The point is not perfect execution but repeated attention to something that is already passing. You can practice at the same time each day or whenever you prepare a drink, whichever fits your schedule better.
